papers.title_in_file: Hand-waving and Interpretive Dance: An Introductory Course on Tensor Networks (Lecture Notes), arXiv:1603.03039v4
sections_read: 1 Introduction to Tensor Network Notation (1.1 Tensors, 1.2 Tensor operations, Aside 1, 1.3 Tensor networks, 1.4 Bubbling, 1.5 Computational Complexity, Problems 1, 1.7 References)

2 Quantum information examples (2.1 Bell state and the Bell basis, 2.2 Quantum Teleportation, 2.2.1 Gate Teleportation, 2.3 Purification, 2.4 Stinespring's Dilation Theorem, Problems 2, 2.6 References)

3 Matrix Product States (3.1 1D Projected Entangled Pair States, 3.2 Some MPS states, 3.3 MPS Properties, 3.4 Renormalising Matrix Product States, 3.5 Mixed States and Many Body Operators, Problems 3, 3.7 References)
4 Classifying Gapped Phases in 1D (4.1 Quantum Phases, 4.2 Injective MPS, 4.3 No Topological Order, 4.4 Symmetry Respecting Phases, Lemma 1, Lemma 2, Theorem 1, Aside 2, Problems 4, 4.6 References)
5 Tensor network algorithms (5.1 DMRG, 5.1.1 One-site, 5.1.2 Two-site, 5.2 TEBD, 5.3 Implementation, Problems 5, 5.5 References)

6 Projected Entangled Pair States (6.1 One Dimensional Systems: MPS, 6.2 Extending to Higher Dimensions, 6.3 Some PEPS examples, Aside 3, 6.4 2D Cluster State and the complexity of PEPS, 6.4.1 Numerical PEPS, 6.5 Properties of PEPS, Aside 4, 6.5.1 Algebraic decay of correlations, 6.5.2 Gauge freedom, Problems 6, 6.7 References)
7 Multiscale Entanglement Renormalisation Ansatz (7.1 Properties of MERA, 7.2 Renormalisation Group Transformation, 7.3 AdS/CFT, 7.4 Some Simple MERA States, Problems 7, 7.6 References)
Appendix A PEPOs for local Hamiltonians: The 'particle decay' construction (A.1 1D, A.2 2D and higher, A.3 Other examples, A.4 References)

papers.what_it_is: A seven-lecture introductory course (lecture notes) on tensor networks: notation, quantum information examples, MPS, classification of 1D gapped phases, DMRG and TEBD, PEPS, and MERA.

assertions.value: The authors state that the notes form the basis for a seven lecture course that introduces the basics of a range of common tensor networks and algorithms.
quotes: These notes form the basis for a seven lecture course, introducing the basics of a range of common tensor networks and algorithms.
assertions.certainty_reason: The abstract states the scope of the notes.

assertions.value: The authors state that the lectures are intended to be generally accessible, although the relevance of many examples may be lost on students without a background in many-body physics or quantum information.
quotes: The lectures are intended to be generally accessible, although the relevance of many of the examples may be lost on students without a background in many-body physics/quantum information.
assertions.certainty_reason: The abstract states the intended audience and its own limit.

assertions.value: The authors state that much of the material was reproduced from memory after one of the authors attended the Tensor Network Summer School at Universiteit Gent in 2015.
quotes: Much of the material was reproduced from memory after one of the authors attended the Tensor Network Summer School at Universiteit Gent in 2015.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state how the material was produced.
assertions.reader_inference: Lecture notes written partly from memory are a secondary teaching source, not a primary derivation.

assertions.value: The authors state that one of the biggest obstacles to the theoretical and numerical study of quantum many-body systems is the curse of dimensionality, the exponential growth of the Hilbert space of quantum states.
quotes: One of the biggest obstacles to the theoretical and numerical study of quantum many-body systems is the curse of dimensionality, the exponential growth of the Hilbert space of quantum states.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement in the introduction, with no evidence given in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that tensor networks have proven to be an incredibly important technique in studying condensed matter systems, with much of the modern theory and numerics involving tensor networks.
quotes: Tensor networks have proven to be an incredibly important technique in studying condensed matter systems, with much of the modern theory and numerics used to study these systems involving tensor networks.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without evidence in the notes.

assertions.value: The authors state that DMRG and TEBD are particularly prevalent algorithms and have become standard tools in numerical many-body physics.
quotes: We introduce two such algorithms, namely DMRG and TEBD, which are particularly prevalent. These have become standard tools in numerical many-body physics.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement about the field, without evidence in the notes.

assertions.value: The authors define a tensor network as a diagram that tells how to combine several tensors into a single composite tensor, whose rank is the number of unmatched legs, and whose value for a given configuration of external indices is the product of the constituent tensor values summed over all consistent internal index labellings.
quotes: A tensor network is a diagram which tells us how to combine several tensors into a single composite tensor.
The rank of this overall tensor is given by the number of unmatched legs in the diagram.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the term in Section 1.3.

assertions.value: The authors state that grouping the contracted and uncontracted indices reduces tensor contraction to matrix multiplication, and that this is the manner in which numerical tensor packages perform contraction, so they can use highly optimised matrix multiplication code.
quotes: It should be noted that not only is this reduction to matrix multiplication pedagogically handy, but this is precisely the manner in which numerical tensor packages perform contraction, allowing them to leverage highly optimised matrix multiplication code.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement about software practice, with no evidence in the notes.

assertions.value: The authors cite Eckart and Young for the result that, measuring error in the Frobenius norm, trimming the singular value decomposition is an ideal low matrix-rank approximation.
quotes: Eckart and Young [1] showed that if we measure error in the Frobenius norm, then trimming the singular value decomposition is an ideal approximation.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the notes attribute to other work and do not prove.
assertions.reader_inference: The Eckart-Young theorem is textbook-standard; the low grade reflects that the notes cite it without proof.

assertions.value: The authors cite Mirsky for a generalisation of the Eckart-Young result that shows optimality of the trimmed singular value decomposition in all unitarily invariant norms.
quotes: Mirsky further generalised this result in Ref. [2] to show optimality in all unitarily invariant norms.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the notes attribute to other work and do not prove.

assertions.value: The authors state that for a ladder-shaped network, contracting each rung in turn keeps the tracked tensor at rank never more than 3, giving constant memory and linear time costs, whereas contracting along the top and then the bottom needs exponential memory and time.
quotes: n, and thus the number of entries is scaling exponentially with n. As such the memory and time footprints of this contraction are also exponential, rendering it infeasible for large n.
If however we contract each rung in turn, the tracked tensor has a rank never more than 3, giving constant memory and linear time costs.
assertions.certainty_reason: A worked argument in lecture notes with no formal statement; the first quote starts mid-sentence on the next page.

assertions.value: The authors state that the 2D grid network admits no efficient contraction ordering, because the contracted region must, somewhere near the middle of the procedure, have a perimeter on the order of the square root of the number of tensors, so such contractions generically take exponential time and memory.
quotes: some networks possess an underlying graph structure that does not admit any eﬃcient contraction ordering. A good example of this is the 2D grid
As a result such contractions generically take exponential time/memory to perform.
assertions.certainty_reason: A heuristic argument by the authors for single-tensor bubbling, not a formal proof.

assertions.value: The authors state that the code of Ref. [3] finds optimal bubbling order for networks of up to 30-40 tensors.
quotes: Ref. [3] provides code which allows for ﬁnding optimal bubbling order for networks of up to 30-40 tensors.
assertions.certainty_reason: A capability of other work, cited without evidence.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing prior work, that the underlying problem of finding a good contraction order (bubbling) for a tensor network is NP-complete.
quotes: the underlying computational problem is NP-complete [6, 7]
assertions.certainty_reason: A hardness result the notes attribute to other work.

assertions.value: The authors argue that contracting the tensor network built from a graph (an e tensor at each vertex, an n tensor in the middle of each edge) gives the number of vertex q-colourings, and so, since existence of a q-colouring is NP-complete, contracting this network is #P-complete.
quotes: If each index is q-dimensional this is a vertex q-colouring of the graph, and the value of the tensor network corresponds to the number of such q-colourings.
contracting this graph is therefore #P-complete [9]
assertions.certainty_reason: The construction is given in outline and rests on cited complexity results; the statement is not set out as a theorem with conditions.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing a quantum hardness result, that approximate contraction of tensor networks is Post-BQP-hard, which puts it in a class of problems not believed to be efficiently solvable even on a quantum computer.
quotes: there also exists a quantum hardness result which shows approximate contraction to be Post-BQP-hard, putting it inside a class of problems not believed to be eﬃciently solvable on even a quantum computer.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result attributed to other work (the notes point to Section 6).

assertions.value: The authors state that the Bell basis corresponds to a vectorisation of the Pauli operators, with the Euclidean inner product on Bell basis states corresponding to the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product on Paulis.
quotes: Thus we see that the Bell basis is intimately linked to the Pauli operators, with the Euclidean inner product on Bell basis states corresponding to the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product on Paulis.
assertions.certainty_reason: A short derivation in the notes whose statement is given loosely, without stated conditions.

assertions.value: The authors show in tensor network notation that teleportation delivers the state correctly for any Bell measurement outcome p, each outcome seen with probability one quarter, so the overall procedure is deterministic despite non-deterministic intermediate states.
quotes: is seen with probability 1/4.
Thus we see that in spite of the non-deterministic intermediary states, the overall procedure is deterministic.
assertions.certainty_reason: The statement is a textbook result derived in the notes, but its conditions are not quoted as a theorem; the first quote is the end of a sentence.

assertions.value: The authors state that in gate teleportation, when U is a Clifford operator the correction is also a Pauli, so the procedure is no more resource intensive in terms of gates used than standard teleportation.
quotes: If U is a Cliﬀord operator2, this correction is also a Pauli, making the procedure no more resource intensive in terms of the gates used than standard teleportation.
assertions.certainty_reason: A short derivation whose conditions are stated informally.

assertions.value: The authors state Stinespring's theorem: any quantum channel, a completely positive trace preserving map, can be expressed as a unitary map V acting on a larger system followed by a partial trace, and they derive it in tensor network notation from Kraus operators.
quotes: Stinespring’s Theorem says that any quantum channel E – a completely positive trace preserving (CPTP) map – can be expressed as a unitary map V acting on a larger system followed by a partial trace
Using this, and partial tracing over the upper index, we get the Stinespring Dilation Theorem as desired:
assertions.certainty_reason: The statement and its condition (a CPTP map) are quoted, and the notes derive it in Eqs. (2.19) to (2.23).

assertions.value: The authors define the alpha-Renyi entropy and state that the entanglement rank S0 is the log of the number of nonzero Schmidt weights, and that the von Neumann entropy is recovered for alpha tending to 1.
quotes: Note that the entanglement rank S0 is simply the (log of the) number of nonzero Schmidt weights and the von Neumann entropy is recovered for α → 1.
assertions.certainty_reason: The notes define the entropy family and its special cases in Section 3.

assertions.value: The authors state that any state with a strong area law S0 ≤ log c for some constant c along any bipartition can be expressed exactly as an MPS with only O(dN c squared) coefficients.
quotes: any state with a so-called strong area law such that S0 ≤ log c for some constant c along any bipartition can be expressed (exactly) using an MPS with only O(dN c2) coeﬃcients.
assertions.certainty_reason: The statement and its condition are quoted; it follows from the exact SVD construction the section sets out.
assertions.reader_inference: The exponent in c2 is printed flat in the text layer; read as c squared.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing prior work, that for many relevant states an area law for the von Neumann entropy, S1 = O(1), suffices to guarantee arbitrarily good approximation by an MPS of only polynomial bond dimension.
quotes: an area law for the von Neumann entropy (S1 = O(1)) is suﬃcient to guarantee arbitrarily good approximation with an MPS of only poly(N ) bond dimension [1–3].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the notes attribute to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the PEPS construction of an MPS should not generally be seen as a practical preparation procedure, because generically the PEPS tensors map states into a non-trivial subspace, which needs post-selected measurements, so the procedure is not generally scalable.
quotes: Generically the PEPS tensors will map states down into a non-trivial subspace, with the physical implementation of this requiring post-selected measurements.
meaning this procedure is not generally scalable.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit of the construction as a preparation procedure.

assertions.value: The authors state that for the AKLT state, with the Hamiltonian built from the projector onto the spin-2 subspace of a pair of spin-1 particles, the ground state is unique and gapped on periodic boundary conditions.
quotes: Let Π2 be the projector onto the spin-2 subspace of a pair of spin-1 particles.
It is simple to check that on periodic boundary conditions the ground state of H = Π2 is unique (and gapped).
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors say it is simple to check and give no proof in the notes.

assertions.value: The authors state that for the cluster state the PEPS tensor corresponds to a unitary circuit, one of the exceptional cases in which the PEPS description can be considered a scalable preparation procedure.
quotes: Notice in this case our PEPS tensor P simply corresponds to unitary circuit.
As such this is one of the exceptional cases in which the PEPS description can be considered a scalable preparation procedure.
assertions.certainty_reason: A short derivation in lecture notes with no formal statement or stated conditions.

assertions.value: The authors argue that, with A normalised so the dominant eigenvalue of the transfer matrix E is 1 and the rest inside the unit disk, any correlator either decays exponentially with distance or is constant, so MPS can only capture states with exponentially decaying correlations.
quotes: We can normalise A so that the dominant eigenvalue of E is 1, with the rest lying inside the unit disk.
Thus we see that MPS can only capture states with exponentially decaying correlations [6].
assertions.certainty_reason: The statement and its setting (a normalised MPS tensor and its transfer matrix) are quoted, and Section 3.3.1 gives the argument through Eq. (3.41).

assertions.value: The authors state that not all MPS represent different physical states, and that gauge transformations, basis transformations on the virtual level, leave the physical state invariant; M need only have a left inverse, so it can be rectangular and enlarge the bond dimension.
quotes: Not all MPS represent diﬀerent physical states [2].
In the case of MPS, these correspond to basis transformations on the virtual level:
Note that M is only required to have a left inverse, so can be rectangular and enlarge the bond dimension.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines gauge transformations of an MPS in Section 3.3.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that blocking MPS sites is a product of transfer matrices and that the dimension of the blocked transfer matrix stays D to the fourth power (printed D4) at all times, so no degrees of freedom need to be discarded.
quotes: Note that the dimension of E˜ remains D4 at all times, so we never need to worry about discarding degrees of freedom.
assertions.certainty_reason: A brief statement in the notes without a formal statement of conditions.
assertions.reader_inference: The exponent in D4 is printed flat in the text layer; read as D to the fourth.

assertions.value: The authors state that MPOs can represent a large class of many body operators, including small depth quantum circuits and local Hamiltonians, and, more generally, any operator that does not increase the Schmidt rank of any state too much.
quotes: In addition to being used to represent density matrices, MPOs can be used to represent a large class of many body operators, including small depth quantum circuits and local Hamiltonians.
More generally, an MPO can be used to represent any operator which does not increase the Schmidt rank of any state too much.
assertions.certainty_reason: A general statement in the notes, illustrated by examples but not proved.

assertions.value: The authors define two states as in the same phase if there is a continuous family of Hamiltonians H(λ) such that one state is the ground state of H(0), the other is the ground state of H(1), and the gap remains open for all λ in [0, 1].
quotes: we will say that two states |ψ0 and |ψ1 are in the same phase if there is a continuous family of Hamiltonians H(λ) such that |ψ0 is the ground state of H(0), |ψ1 is the ground state of H(1), and the gap remains open for all λ ∈ [0, 1].
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the definition it uses for a quantum phase.

assertions.value: The authors state that it is simpler, and essentially equivalent, to ask which states can be interconverted by a local quantum circuit of depth constant in the system size, and that they work within this framework.
quotes: It is simpler, and essentially equivalent, to ask which states can be interconverted by a local quantum circuit of depth constant in the system size [3, 4].
assertions.certainty_reason: An equivalence the notes attribute to other work and do not prove.

assertions.value: The authors state that the lecture restricts itself to injective MPS, defined as MPS in left canonical form for which the identity is the unique eigenvalue 1 left eigenvector of the transfer matrix, and that the arguments generalise to non-injective MPS but become very technical.
quotes: In this lecture, we will restrict ourselves to the case of injective MPS [7, 8].
then injective MPS are those for which the identity is the unique eigenvalue 1 left eigenvector of the transfer matrix.
The arguments we will present here generalise to non-injective MPS, however they become very technical.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scope and definition in Section 4.2.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing prior work, that injective MPS correspond to unique gapped ground states of local Hamiltonians.
quotes: These MPS correspond to unique gapped ground states of local Hamiltonians [9].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the notes attribute to other work.

assertions.value: The authors argue that all injective MPS are in the same (topological) phase as the product state, and therefore each other, since blocking a constant number of sites gives a constant depth circuit that disentangles the MPS, so there are no nontrivial topological phases in 1D.
quotes: In fact, we will see that there are no nontrivial topological phases in 1D [3].
Let Aj deﬁne some injective MPS, and construct the transfer matrix E6
Notice that this was all achieved by simply blocking a constant number of sites together, so we have
Therefore, all injective MPS are in the same (topological) phase as the product state, and therefore each other.
assertions.certainty_reason: The statement is quoted with its condition (injective MPS) and Section 4.3 gives the argument; the equivalence notion is the constant depth circuit of Section 4.1.

assertions.value: The paper proves Lemma 1: for a unitary u and an injective MPS tensor A, the largest eigenvalue λ of the u-transfer matrix is contained within the unit disk, that is |λ| ≤ 1.
quotes: Lemma 1. Let u be some unitary and A an injective MPS tensor. Then the largest eigenvalue λ of the u-transfer matrix
is contained within the unit disk.
and so |λ| ≤ 1.
assertions.certainty_reason: The statement and its conditions are quoted and the proof, by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, is in Section 4.4.

assertions.value: The paper proves Lemma 2: equality is achieved in Lemma 1 if and only if there exists a unitary v and an angle θ such that u can be pushed through the MPS tensor as in Eqn. 4.19; the proof uses injectivity to show v is unitary after rescaling.
quotes: Lemma 2. Equality is achieved in Lemma 1 if and only if there exists a unitary v and an angle θ such that
Assume that Eqn. 4.19 holds.
Thus we conclude v is, after rescaling, unitary, and that Eqn. 4.19 therefore holds.
assertions.certainty_reason: The statement and its conditions are quoted and the proof is in Section 4.4; the equation itself is garbled in the text layer.

assertions.value: The paper proves Theorem 1 (Symmetries push through): for a group G, a unitary representation ug is a local symmetry if and only if it pushes through the MPS tensor as a unitary vg and a phase, with vg unitary and θg in [0, 2π).
quotes: Theorem 1 (Symmetries push through). Let G be a group. A unitary representation ug is a local symmetry if and only if
for vg unitary and θg ∈ [0, 2π).
which completes the proof.
assertions.certainty_reason: The statement and its conditions are quoted and the proof is given in Section 4.4, within the injective MPS scope.

assertions.value: The authors state that pushing a symmetry action through a symmetric constant depth circuit and onto the virtual level means any properties of the virtual action will be an invariant of the phase.
quotes: Therefore, any properties it has will be an invariant of the phase.
assertions.certainty_reason: A one-line argument in the notes without a formally stated theorem.

assertions.value: The authors state that there are projective representations that are not equivalent to any linear representation, and that the reader will show this in Problems 4.
quotes: As you will show in Problems 4, there are projective representations which are not equivalent to any linear representation.
assertions.certainty_reason: The proof is left as an exercise, so no proof is given in the notes.

assertions.value: The authors state that the only freedom to change vg within a phase is local rephasing, so the equivalence classes of ω label the different phases of injective MPS with a symmetry restriction, and these classes are indexed by the second group cohomology class H2(G, U (1)) of the group G.
quotes: the equivalence classes of ω label the diﬀerent phases of injective MPS with a symmetry restriction.
so-called second group cohomology class of the group G, an object usually written as H2(G, U (1)) [2, 10].
assertions.certainty_reason: The notes give an argument and cite the classification to other work; the statement is not set out as a theorem with conditions.
assertions.reader_inference: The exponent in H2 is printed flat in the text layer; it is the second cohomology group.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing prior work, that finding ground states of one-dimensional spin systems, even with a local Hamiltonian, retains QMA-completeness, which dashes any hope of general simulation even on a quantum computer.
quotes: Even under the assumption of a local Hamiltonian, this seemingly narrow problem retains QMA-completeness [1] (a quantum analogue of NP), dashing any hope of general simulation, even on a quantum computer.
assertions.certainty_reason: A hardness result the notes attribute to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing prior work, that the presence of a gap makes ground states of local Hamiltonians efficiently approximable, so the complexity drops from QMA-complete all the way down to P, removing the complexity barrier to simulation.
quotes: showing that the presence of the gap causes the complexity to plummet from QMA-complete all the way down to P, removing the complexity barrier to simulation.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result attributed to other work in the notes.

assertions.value: The authors state that the ground state is approximated by minimising the Rayleigh quotient of the Hamiltonian over a restricted domain, here MPS of bounded bond dimension, with DMRG and TEBD differing in how the variation step is performed.
quotes: the way in which we plan to approximate the ground state is by minimising the Rayleigh quotient of the Hamiltonian H (the energy) over some restricted domain D
we will restrict ourselves to the domain D of MPS of a bounded bond dimension.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the setup of the algorithms it presents.

assertions.value: The authors state that DMRG is by far the most studied and successful of the algorithms in the field.
quotes: By far the most studied and successful of the algorithms in the ﬁeld is DMRG.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without evidence in the notes.

assertions.value: The authors state that the key heuristic behind DMRG is to exploit the simplicity of the local problems, approximating the multi-tensor optimisation by iterated single-tensor optimisations.
quotes: key heuristic behind DMRG is to exploit the simplicity of these local problems, approximating the multivariate (multi-tensor) optimisation by iterated univariate (single tensor) optimisations.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper describes the algorithm it presents.

assertions.value: The authors state that, with the MPS in canonical form, each one-site DMRG step has a closed form solution given by the minimum eigenvector of the Hermitian environment tensor, and that sweeping back and forth along the chain completes the algorithm.
quotes: As Hi is Hermitian, this optimisation has a closed form solution given by the minimum eigenvector9 of Hi.
By sweeping back and forth along the chain, solving this localised eigenvector problem, and then shifting along the canonicalisation as necessary, we complete our description of the algorithm.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the algorithm it presents.

assertions.value: The authors state that DMRG1 keeps the state within the MPS manifold without the bond dimension growing, so the algorithm is greedy, but that this means there is no particularly convenient method of gently growing the bond dimension and no information is gained about the appropriateness of the bond dimension chosen.
quotes: The main advantage of DMRG1 is that the state stays within the MPS manifold without the bond dimension growing, meaning that the algorithm is greedy10.
there is no particularly convenient method of gently growing the bond dimension as the algorithm runs11, and no information is gained
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limitation of the algorithm they present.

assertions.value: The authors state that the splitting step gives DMRG2 its power, allowing dynamic control of the bond dimension and information about the error caused by trimming, which helps inform the choice of bond dimension.
quotes: This splitting process gives DMRG2 its power, allowing for dynamic control of the bond dimension, as well as providing information about the amount of error caused by trimming
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement about algorithm behaviour, without evidence in the notes.

assertions.value: The authors state that time-evolving block decimation (TEBD) simulates the dynamics of 1D spin systems, and that by simulating imaginary-time-evolution low-temperature features such as the ground state may be calculated as well.
quotes: is a tensor network algorithm that allows the dynamics of 1D spin systems to be simulated.
By simulating imaginary-time-evolution low-temperature features such as the ground state may be calculated as well.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author description of the algorithm's use, without evidence in the notes.

assertions.value: The authors state that while H has a constant Schmidt rank and an efficient MPO representation, the imaginary-time-evolution operator U(τ) generically has exponential bond dimension.
quotes: Whilst H has a constant Schmidt rank, admitting an eﬃcient representation as an MPO, U (τ ) generically has exponential bond dimension
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement in the notes without proof; the quote stops before the qualifier for almost all τ.

assertions.value: The authors state that the first order exponential product approximation is the Suzuki-Trotter formula, which evolves each subsystem in turn and has error O(τ squared): e−τ(A+B) = e−τA e−τB + O(τ2).
quotes: The central mathematical tool to TEBD are the exponential product approximations. The ﬁrst
order of these approximation is the Suzuki-Trotter formula, which approximates the total evolution
e−τ (A+B) = e−τAe−τB + O(τ 2) .
assertions.certainty_reason: A standard approximation presented without derivation in the notes.
assertions.reader_inference: The exponent in the error term is printed as O(τ 2); read as tau squared.

assertions.value: The authors state that because the TEBD procedure is entirely localised, TEBD admits a large amount of parallelisation not typically available to DMRG.
quotes: As the above procedure is entirely localised, TEBD also admits a large amount of parallelisation, not typically available to DMRG.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without evidence in the notes.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing prior work, that the Local Hamiltonian problem is in P for 1D gapped Hamiltonians.
quotes: It is known that the Local Hamiltonian problem is in P for 1D gapped Hamiltonians [8– 12].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result attributed to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that PEPS is a misnomer in two ways: there is not necessarily a projector and there is not necessarily an entangled pair.
quotes: We will see how this is a misnomer in two ways, there is not necessarily a projector and there is not necessarily an entangled pair.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement previewing the section, with no evidence beyond the discussion.

assertions.value: The authors state that PEPS built on entangled triplets offers no more descriptive power than entangled pairs, and that any state preparable from the projected entangled plaquette construction can be prepared from a PEPS at small additional cost.
quotes: Clearly this doesn’t oﬀer any more descriptive power than using entangled pairs.
so any state which can be prepared from this ‘projected entangled plaquette’ construction can be prepared from a PEPS at small additional cost.
assertions.certainty_reason: Short constructive arguments in the notes without stated conditions.

assertions.value: The authors construct a Hamiltonian from vertex terms and plaquette terms on a square lattice whose ground state is an equal superposition over all closed loop states, the ground state of Kitaev's toric code.
quotes: The ground state of this Hamiltonian is the superposition of all closed loops of ﬂipped spins.
and the ground state is an equal superposition over all closed loop states:
assertions.certainty_reason: A construction argued in the notes, not set out as a theorem with conditions.

assertions.value: The authors state that the toric code PEPS tensor, with an even number of virtual bonds in the |1 state for a nonzero entry, has a property called G-injectivity, a symmetry on the virtual level that is closely related to the topological order in this model.
quotes: Since an even number of the virtual bonds must be in the |1 state for the tensor entry to be nonzero, the PEPS tensor has a property called G-injectivity [6].
This turns out to be closely related to the topological order present in this model.
assertions.certainty_reason: The property is attributed to other work and described without proof.

assertions.value: The authors state that a PEPS tensor with bond dimension D = 2 and the listed nonzero elements generates the 2D cluster state, a universal resource for measurement based quantum computing.
quotes: Let D = 2 be the bond dimension and let
The physical state generated is the 2D cluster state, a universal resource for measurement based quantum computing [7, 8].
assertions.certainty_reason: The construction is given, but verification is left to Problem 6.3; the universality claim is cited.

assertions.value: The authors argue that, since efficient inner products between PEPS would let a classical computer simulate post-selected single qubit measurements, simple PEPS states cannot be contracted efficiently unless post-selected quantum computing can be classically simulated (Post-BQP=BPP).
quotes: This shows us that we cannot contract even simple PEPS states eﬃciently, unless post-selected quantum computing can be classically simulated (Post-BQP=BPP) [9].
assertions.certainty_reason: A hardness result the notes attribute to other work and sketch only.

assertions.value: The authors state that, in many practical situations, approximate contraction of PEPS networks can be achieved in both the finite and infinite system size limits.
quotes: In many practical situations, approximate contraction of PEPS networks can be achieved in both the ﬁnite [10] and inﬁnite [11, 12] system size limits.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement attributed to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the PEPS built from a classical partition function is a pure state, not a thermal state, that is not normalised with ⟨ψ|ψ⟩ = Z, and that correlation functions computed with it equal those of classical statistical physics.
quotes: Note this is a pure state, and not a thermal state. It is however not normalised, with ψ|ψ = Z.
assertions.certainty_reason: A construction described in the notes, not set out as a theorem with conditions.

assertions.value: The authors argue that a classical model with a thermal phase transition, such as the Ising model, shows algebraic decay of correlations at the critical temperature, so the corresponding PEPS does too, and that unlike MPS, PEPS states can exhibit algebraic decay of correlations.
quotes: Such a model will exhibit algebraic decay of correlations at the critical temperature, implying that the corresponding PEPS does as well.
Thus we can see that unlike MPS, the states described by PEPS can exhibit algebraic decay of correlations.
assertions.certainty_reason: An argument by reduction to a classical model, stated without conditions as a theorem.

assertions.value: The authors state that, unlike for MPS, a PEPS cannot exactly be brought into a canonical form, though numerical methods exist to bring PEPS into approximate canonical forms.
quotes: This cannot be done exactly in the case of PEPS, though there do exist numerical methods to bring PEPS into approximate canonical forms [13].
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement attributed to other work without proof in the notes.

assertions.value: The authors state that MPS always have exponentially decaying correlations whereas gapless ground states generically support power law decay, and that MPS have a strict area law for entanglement entropy whereas gapless states admit a logarithmic divergence.
quotes: Recall that MPS always have exponentially decaying correlations, whereas gapless ground states generically support correlations with power law decay.
Similarly MPS also have a strict area law for entanglement entropy, where gapless states admit a logarithmic divergence.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement about gapless states, without evidence in the notes.

assertions.value: The authors state that, unlike PEPS, the MERA network can be efficiently optimised in higher dimensions, although the scaling makes the numerics very challenging.
quotes: Unlike PEPS, the network can be eﬃciently optimised in higher dimensions, although the scaling makes the numerics very challenging!
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without evidence in the notes.

assertions.value: The authors argue by bond counting that removing a block of N physical indices from the rest of a MERA requires cutting O(log N) bonds, so the maximum entropy scales as log N times log D, a logarithmic violation of the area law that MPS cannot realise.
quotes: if n bonds must be broken to separate a region from the rest of the network, the maximum entanglement entropy that can be supported is n log D, where D is the bond dimension.
it is straightforward to see that to remove a block of N physical indices from the rest of the network, O(log N ) bonds must be cut. This shows that the maximum entropy scales as log N log D [1, 2].
assertions.certainty_reason: An upper bound from bond counting, read off a diagram; no theorem with stated conditions.

assertions.value: The authors state that, using the isometric constraints, the length scale behaviour of a two point correlator on a MERA is determined by a superoperator S, a completely positive, unital map, all of whose eigenvalues satisfy |λ| ≤ 1.
quotes: Using the constraints on the tensors (Eqn. 7.2), we can simplify the evaluation of a two point correlator on a MERA state [3].
Thus, S is a completely positive, unital map and all eigenvalues λ of S are |λ| ≤ 1.
assertions.certainty_reason: An argument in the notes via Kraus operators, not stated as a theorem with conditions.

assertions.value: The authors state that bringing operators separated by N sites together takes about log N applications of S, that the scaling dimensions are defined by ∆φ = − log3 λφ with ∆φ ≥ 0, and that therefore a MERA state can support algebraic decay of correlations.
quotes: operators separated by N sites together by applying S ∼ log N times.
where ∆φ = − log3 λφ, ∆φ ≥ 0 are known as scaling dimensions, where λφ is the corresponding eigenvalue of S.
Therefore, a MERA state can support algebraic decay of correlations.
assertions.certainty_reason: An argument for a ternary MERA with operators at special sites; the notes say it can be easily generalised without showing it.

assertions.value: The authors state that, unlike PEPS, the MERA can be efficiently stored and, thanks to the isometric constraints, local expectation values and correlators can be computed efficiently, because the layers map local operators to local operators and only a causal cone of tensors is needed.
quotes: Although this works for the 1D MPS network, it fails for 2D PEPS states; the contractions required to calculate expectation values of local operators is incredibly hard.

It turns out the MERA has both of these properties. One can eﬃciently store the state data, and, thanks to the constraints in Eqn. 7.2, one can eﬃciently compute local expectation values and correlators.
assertions.certainty_reason: An argument in the notes without a theorem with stated conditions.

assertions.value: The authors state that, for the ternary MERA, after a single layer of tensors a local operator becomes a three site operator and the range never grows, so the layers map local operators to local operators.
quotes: Indeed, after a single layer of tensors, the operator becomes a three site operator, and the range never grows.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement read from a diagram of the causal cone, without a formal statement.

assertions.value: The authors state that the macroscopic physics, or phase structure, is determined by fixed points of the maps A, and that since there is no characteristic length scale, gapless ground states are expected to be scale invariant.
quotes: Thus, the macroscopic physics, or phase structure, is determined by ﬁxed points of the maps A.
Since there is no characteristic length scale set by either the spectral gap or correlation length, gapless ground states are expected to be scale invariant.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement of expectation, with no proof in the notes.

assertions.value: The authors state that the AdS/MERA connection remains an open research question, and that whether the geometry is best understood as anti-de Sitter or de Sitter is currently unclear.
quotes: We note that the AdS/MERA connection remains an open research question.
Additionally, whether the geometry is best understood as anti-de Sitter [17] or de Sitter [18] is currently unclear.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state an open problem of their own subject.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing prior work, that imposing the graph metric on the MERA gives a discretised anti-de Sitter metric, while the edge theory is a discretised conformal field theory.
quotes: Imposing the graph metric on the MERA, we ﬁnd a discretised anti-de Sitter (AdS) metric [17], whilst the edge theory is a ‘discretised’ CFT.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result attributed to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the cluster state is more conveniently defined on a binary MERA than a ternary one, and that with a top tensor T = |++ the construction gives the cluster state on periodic boundary conditions.
quotes: It is more convenient to deﬁne the cluster state on a binary MERA than a ternary.
If we pick a top tensor T = |++ , we obtain the cluster state on periodic boundary conditions.
assertions.certainty_reason: A construction stated without a derivation; verification is left to the problems.

assertions.value: The authors report, for the transverse field cluster model from a numerically optimised ternary MERA, that the Hamiltonian remains gapless over a range of λ, over which the ground state energy varies continuously, and that the decay exponents also vary, so the RG fixed point depends on λ.
quotes: The Hamiltonian remains gapless for a range of values of λ, over which the ground state energy varies continuously as seen in Fig. 1a).
The decay exponents also vary over this range, meaning that the thermodynamic physics or RG ﬁxed point is dependent on λ.
assertions.certainty_reason: Results reproduced from Ref. [29], an empirical result from one study, reported without numerical detail in the text.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 1a: the ground state energy density E0 of the transverse field cluster model from an optimised ternary MERA falls smoothly with λ, from about -2.1 at the left end (λ about -0.7) to about -3.5 at λ about 1, and the MERA points lie on the exact curve at the scale of the plot.
quotes: Figure 1: a) Ground state energy density extracted from a ternary MERA after optimising the tensors to locally minimise the energy.
Figures reproduced from Ref. [29].
assertions.certainty_reason: A value read from a figure, reproduced from other work.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 1b: the correlation decay exponents (scaling dimensions) from the ternary MERA follow the exact lines closely over λ from about -0.7 to about 1, in a band from zero to about 2, with a nonzero lowest branch that starts near about 1/2 and more scatter among the upper branches.
quotes: b) Correlation decay exponents for the transverse ﬁeld cluster model obtained from a ternary MERA.
Figures reproduced from Ref. [29].
assertions.certainty_reason: A value read from a figure, reproduced from other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that an analytic MPO construction is known in 1D for highly structured Hamiltonians, such as local and translation invariant ones, and that the appendix reviews it and outlines a generalisation that expresses local Hamiltonians optimally as PEPOs in arbitrary spatial dimensions.
quotes: an analytic MPO construction of such operators is known in 1D [1].

In this section we review this, and outline a generalisation which allows for local Hamiltonians (and even slightly less structured operators) to be optimally expressed as a PEPOs in arbitrary spatial dimensions.
assertions.certainty_reason: The appendix states what it covers.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the particle decay picture, the automaton can go from the right-moving particle to the vacuum either directly, giving the field term −hZ, or via an intermediate state 1, giving the Ising term −JXX, at any location.
quotes: With only these restrictions, the automaton can transition from |→ to |· either directly (giving the ﬁeld term −hZ), or via 1 (giving the Ising term −JXX) at any location.
assertions.certainty_reason: A construction for a single example, not stated as a general theorem.

assertions.value: The authors state that by introducing intermediary states and different decay rules, arbitrary local Hamiltonians in any dimension can be similarly constructed.
quotes: As with 1D, by introducing intermediary states and diﬀerent decay rules, arbitrary local Hamiltonians in any dimension can be similarly constructed.
assertions.certainty_reason: A general claim supported only by examples in the appendix.
